issues.subcategory: Differential and large-scale exclusion based on outcome-related variable
issues.description: Across all experiments, participants were excluded for having 'too few high confidence critical trials.' This is exclusion based on a variable (high confidence response rate) that is intrinsically related to the dependent measure and the constructs of interest. In Experiment 1, 17 of 40 participants (42.5%) were excluded; in Experiment 2, 92 of 290 (31.7%) were excluded. Excluding nearly half the sample on a confidence-related criterion can systematically bias the remaining sample toward participants who are generally overconfident, which could inflate the prevalence of high-confidence illusions and undermine the core claim that illusions are 'high confidence.' The dramatic difference in high-confidence rates between included and excluded groups (e.g., 53.8% vs 26.2% in Exp 1) confirms the exclusion strongly reshaped the sample.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions. Included participants had on average 53.8% high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: 36.3 – 93.2, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent reported illusion rates between Results and Discussion
issues.description: The Results section of Experiment 1 reports the increase in illusory errors as going from 19% (short) to 26% (averaged over short-with-interference and long), and separately reports pseudo-letter illusions increasing from 29% to 41%. However, the Experiment 1 Discussion reports the high confidence expectation-induced illusions increasing 'from 29% to 39% and 43%, respectively,' and the General Discussion and Discussion mention figures like 43% and 50%. These different numerical summaries for the same conditions are not clearly reconciled, making it difficult to verify which values correspond to which cells.
issues.quote: the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%, respectively.

issues.subcategory: Internally inconsistent three-way interaction interpretation in Experiment 4
issues.description: The text states 'There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).' A 5% increase is larger than, not smaller than, a 4% increase, so the verbal description contradicts the numbers. Additionally, elsewhere illusory increases are described as 14% to 19% overall (a 5% increase), making the per-target-type decomposition (5% vs 4%) hard to reconcile.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.subcategory: Missing pre-registration and undisclosed analytic choices
issues.description: Although the manuscript frames three a priori hypotheses and uses sequential Bayesian stopping rules in Experiments 3 and 4, no pre-registration is mentioned for any experiment. Key analytic decisions (the 10-trial exclusion threshold, the choice to collapse over set size in Exp 1, collapsing over cue color in Exp 2, the prior width for the Bayesian ANOVAs, and the default JASP Cauchy prior scale) are not justified or reported. The exclusion threshold in particular appears to be a researcher degree of freedom that strongly affects sample composition.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less)

issues.subcategory: Sequential testing stopping rule details incomplete
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used an optional-stopping rule based on a sequential Bayes Factor crossing 10 for a 'critical t-test,' checked every other testing day. However, the minimum sample size, maximum sample size, exact comparison used for the stopping rule, and whether the stopping rule was decided before data collection are not fully specified. Optional stopping with Bayes Factors mitigates but does not fully eliminate flexibility concerns, and the lack of detail (e.g., no specified cap) limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Failure of key manipulation (transient expectation) undermines a central claim
issues.description: Experiment 2's cue-color manipulation (inducing transient expectations) showed no effect (BFincl = 0.07), which the authors interpret post hoc as evidence that 'expectations need substantial time to develop.' However, this null could equally reflect that the manipulation was too weak, that participants did not learn the contingency (indeed none reported it in the questionnaire), or that the implicit association was never acquired. Without a manipulation check confirming participants acquired the color-probability association, the null result cannot distinguish 'transient expectations don't work' from 'the manipulation failed.'
issues.quote: However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories. This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.subcategory: Confidence rating scale conflates 'guess' anchor with confidence construct
issues.description: The confidence scale is anchored 1 = guess, 4 = certain, and the central analytic distinction rests on isolating 'high confidence' trials. However, the manuscript does not state how high-confidence was operationalized (e.g., ratings of 4 only, or 3 and 4). Whether '4' alone or '3-4' counts as high confidence materially changes which trials enter the analysis and the illusion rates reported. This operationalization is essential to the central claim that errors are genuine memory illusions rather than guesses, yet it is left unspecified.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain).

issues.subcategory: Decay/interference confound with response competition not fully excluded
issues.description: The increase in illusions over the retention interval is interpreted as evidence that illusions arise 'during STM storage.' However, an alternative is that longer delays simply increase overall memory uncertainty at the decision/retrieval stage, where strong priors then bias the choice among response options — a retrieval-stage rather than a storage-stage process. The authors' own predictive-processing discussion acknowledges 'prediction-related effects at retrieval' as a possibility, which contradicts the strong claim that the effect 'must be due to processes ongoing in STM' storage. The data cannot distinguish storage-stage rewriting from retrieval-stage biasing.
issues.quote: This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.subcategory: Interference manipulation confounds delay and interference; 'WM vs FM' mapping is loose
issues.description: In Experiment 1 the 'Short with interference' condition presents the second display together with the cue, while in the 'Short' condition it appears 5 s after memory offset. The authors map the interference condition onto a 'WM manipulation' and the no-interference conditions onto 'FM,' but these mappings are asserted rather than validated. Fragile memory is defined operationally as being destroyed by visual interference; using a single interfering display to claim engagement of distinct memory systems (IM/FM/WM) is a construct-validity overreach, especially since the same letter stimuli and timing differences could produce the effects without invoking separate stores.
issues.quote: Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation, illusory memories are highly prevalent. Experiment 2-4 show that in a FM set-up illusory memories are also abundant.

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralization from letters to visual percepts in general
issues.description: The conclusion extrapolates from highly overlearned, categorical letter stimuli to 'visual percepts in general' and to 'all memory stages,' based partly on speculative reinterpretation of other studies (Chalk et al.). The stimuli are a special case (mirror-reversed letters with extremely strong, lifelong priors and a clear 'correct' canonical form), and the claim that 'very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input' is not supported by the present data, which only test letters.
issues.quote: Secondly, it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general. This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.subcategory: Sample restricted to young university students (and skewed gender) not acknowledged
issues.description: Samples are predominantly young (average ages ~20-22) first-year psychology students, with markedly skewed gender ratios (e.g., Exp 3: 51 women of 64). The strong priors for the Latin alphabet also presume a specific literacy/cultural background that is never characterized. These limitations on generalizability (age, education, literacy, culture) are not discussed, yet the claims are made about human memory in general.
issues.quote: In this experiment, 64 participants participated (51 women; age range 17-46 years, average age 20.5 years), all having normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

issues.subcategory: No perceptual baseline/control to estimate encoding errors directly
issues.description: The entire inferential strategy rests on illusions increasing over time to rule out perceptual/encoding errors, but there is no condition probing memory at or near 0 ms (or a perceptually-available baseline) to directly quantify the perceptual-illusion floor. The shortest delays (500–750 ms) already involve memory, so the proportion of errors attributable to perception versus early memory cannot be cleanly separated; the authors infer a 'mainly correct percept' from the short-delay accuracy rather than measuring it.
issues.quote: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in 70% of high confidence trials, thus showing that initial perceptual encoding was relatively intact.

issues.subcategory: Figure reference error in Experiment 4 results
issues.description: The Experiment 4 Results section opens by referring to 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but Figure 5 belongs to Experiment 3; Experiment 4's data are shown in Figure 6 (as the subsequent figure caption indicates). This mislabeling creates ambiguity about which data are being described.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistency between best-fitting model and reported interaction in Experiment 1
issues.description: The Experiment 1 best model is reported to include the Memory Delay * Error Type interaction, and the text emphasizes this interaction as supporting Hypothesis 2 (BFincl = 4.21). However, BFincl = 4.21 is only 'substantial' evidence and the corresponding inclusion probability shifts are modest (P(incl|data) = 0.660). Given that this is the central test for the time-course claim in Experiment 1, the relatively weak evidence is somewhat overstated in the narrative ('shows support'), and the borderline three-way interaction (BFincl = 2.45) is interpreted substantively despite being only anecdotal.
issues.quote: The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent/uncertain critical-trial counts and design proportions in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1's probabilistic assignment of response options ('83%' real with '16%' mirrored — which sum to 99%, not 100%) and the approximate critical-trial accounting ('~220 trials, 26% of all trials') are imprecise and partly inconsistent. Because critical trials are the basis for all key analyses, exact counts per cell (especially after the high-confidence and exclusion filters) are needed to evaluate power, particularly given the 10-trial-per-cell threshold.
issues.quote: If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.subcategory: Online uncontrolled testing environment in Experiment 4 without stimulus-size control
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online on participants' own laptops via Zoom/Neurotask, yet all stimulus specifications elsewhere are given in degrees of visual angle that depend on viewing distance and screen size, which cannot be controlled online. This undermines comparability with the lab-based Experiments 1–3 and the precision of visual-angle-dependent claims (e.g., visual similarity arguments), and no calibration/viewing-distance procedure is reported.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: Response-bias argument relies on a contestable assumption
issues.description: The authors argue against a response-bias explanation by asserting that a bias should be stronger for low-confidence trials. While plausible, this assumes confidence and bias operate independently and that high-confidence trials reflect genuine memory rather than metacognitive miscalibration aligned with priors. An alternative is that priors simultaneously drive both the response and the (mis)placed confidence, producing exactly the observed pattern (more illusions and higher confidence together) without a 'memory rewriting' mechanism. The logical refutation of response bias is therefore not as decisive as claimed.
issues.quote: If the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias ... should be present not only for the high-confidence responses; indeed, it should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction in Experiment 2 fixation-cross color/probability description
issues.description: Experiment 2 states red cue = pseudo-letter target on 25% of trials and blue cue = pseudo-letter target on 60% of trials. Elsewhere the manuscript frames red as 'indicating a higher probability of a real letter target' (consistent), but the analysis section labels colors as 'red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target,' while the hypothesis text says 'more pseudo-to-real memory illusions should occur after a red fixation cross (indicating a higher probability of a real letter target).' The 25%/60% split is also asymmetric around 50% in an unexplained way, and the rationale for these particular values is not given, complicating interpretation of the null effect.
issues.quote: If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion and per-cell zero-count exclusions handled ad hoc
issues.description: In Experiment 3, 'because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA,' on top of the prior 5 excluded for too few high-confidence trials. The handling of empty cells via listwise deletion (rather than a model robust to missingness) and the cumulative, multi-stage exclusions are not systematically justified, and no sensitivity analysis (e.g., results with all participants or different thresholds) is reported to show robustness.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: Reinterpretation of prior studies as memory (not perceptual) illusions is speculative
issues.description: The Discussion reinterprets De Gardelle et al. and Chalk et al. as likely reflecting memory rather than perceptual illusions. While raising the alternative is legitimate, the manuscript at times states this as 'perhaps a more likely explanation,' which goes beyond what the current data (using different stimuli/paradigms) can establish about those specific studies. The present experiments do not include those paradigms, so causal/explanatory claims about them are unsupported extrapolations.
issues.quote: Moreover, Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that this is perhaps a more likely explanation than an illusion that occurs when perceiving or encoding the stimuli

issues.subcategory: 'World knowledge' versus low-level perceptual familiarity not disentangled
issues.description: The authors attribute the asymmetry (pseudo-to-real >> real-to-pseudo) to 'world knowledge' about letter orientation. However, canonical letters also differ from mirrored letters in low-level perceptual fluency/exposure frequency, which is itself a perceptual-learning variable rather than 'world knowledge' in the conceptual sense invoked. The design cannot separate abstract world-knowledge/expectation from accumulated perceptual exposure to canonical orientations, yet the conclusion privileges the former.
issues.quote: Instead ‘world knowledge’ (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: Set-size manipulation in Experiment 1 underreported and inconsistently described
issues.description: Experiment 1's memory displays varied set size (6 or 8 letters) and pseudo-letter counts, and the figure caption states '1 to 2 pseudo letters (set size 6) or 2 pseudo letters (set size 8),' while the analysis 'averaged across the set size conditions.' Set size is a known major determinant of STM performance, yet it is folded out by averaging without reporting whether illusion effects differ by set size, and without justifying collapsing. This undisclosed collapsing is both a reporting gap and an analytic-flexibility concern.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: Infinite/extreme Bayes Factors reported without scrutiny
issues.description: Several tables report Bayes Factors of ∞ or on the order of 10^13–10^15 (e.g., Table 2 Target Type and Error Type BFincl = ∞; Table 1 BFincl = 1.46e+14). Such extreme/infinite values typically indicate numerical overflow or near-deterministic separation and should be flagged and capped or reported with caution rather than taken at face value; they also suggest the main effects may be driven by structural features of the design (e.g., illusions being a defined subset of errors) rather than substantive variance.

issues.subcategory: Definitional overlap between 'illusions' and 'errors' may inflate key effects
issues.description: Illusory errors are defined as selecting the mirrored counterpart of the target, while 'other errors' are selecting any of several other items. Because the mirrored counterpart is a single, highly specific, perceptually similar option (and in Experiments 2–4 is always present in the response display), the base rate for selecting it differs structurally from selecting 'other' items, which is distributed across multiple alternatives. Comparing a single-target-confusion rate to an aggregated multi-option error rate can mechanically produce a 'main effect of Error Type' independent of any memory illusion, and this asymmetry is not adequately controlled or acknowledged.
issues.quote: Participants were more likely to select the mirrored (pseudo) counterpart of a target than to commit other types of errors (18% vs 11%, main effect of error type, BFinlc>1000)

issues.subcategory: Abstract claims of reliable early-accurate reporting overstate short-delay data
issues.description: The abstract states participants 'go from reliably reporting what was there ... to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected,' implying near-veridical early performance. However, even at the shortest delays illusions are substantial (e.g., ~19–29% in Experiment 1), so the dichotomy between 'reliably reporting what was there' early versus illusions later is overstated relative to the actual effect sizes.
issues.quote: participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there
